The government is therefore prepared to revoke, effective the first day of April, all orders and regulations of the governor in council, with the exceptions I have mentioned. Submission will be made to council promptly to effect such revocation.
I am further prepared to give the undertaking, on behalf of the government, that as soon as the bills to which I have referred receive royal assent, orders and regulations of the governor in council which they replace will be revoked.
It may be that I have been just a little too concise in what I have said. But it may also be that what the government's plans are is perfectly clear. I should like what I have said to stand exactly as I have said it, as the
government's undertaking. Perhaps however I might elaborate a little so as to explain what the plan is.
We have before parliament, at various stages, these bills which I have mentioned. We also have a resolution on the order paper which will be used as the basis for another bill, called the Continuation of Transitional Measures Act; and to that bill will be appended, as I have explained to the house before, a number of orders in council, approximately fifty-five in number.
Now, it is not necessary to continue in force any orders in council which derive their validity from the National Emergency Transitional Powers Act, except those orders in council and regulations which are to be [DOT] appended to the Continuation of Transitional Measures Act, and except the orders in council which are to be replaced by the legislation before the house, namely the list of acts and bills I have mentioned. Therefore the government is prepared to revoke, as of April 1, all orders in council except those I have mentioned. And as soon as the bills I have mentioned receive royal assent, they are also prepared to revoke all orders and regulations which the legislation itself replaces.
I do not know that I need say very much about the necessity for the bill. If we saw any reasonable probability of all this legislation becoming law before March 29, I think we would not ask for this extension. But every one of us knows that it is utterly impossible, in the time that remains before us, between today and March 29, for this legislation to pass its various stages in this house and in the other house, and to receive royal assent.
The matter is so important, and the results would be so disastrous if there were to be an abrupt termination of all these orders and regulations on March 29, that the government has a responsibility to begin-and to begin in time-to see to it that that result does not ensue. That is the reason we are proposing, on this 18th day of March, this address to His Excellency; and a similar address will be introduced in the senate.
I do not think that on this occasion I should outline in any detail the consequences of these orders in council lapsing. However, I might say just in passing that if they do lapse, rent control will disappear; eviction control will disappear; price control will disappear; the supplements to old age pensions now payable under orders in council could no longer be paid, and labour legislation which provides for a system of collective agreements between employers and employees would cease to have any effect. The effect of such an abrupt lapsing of this emergency legislation would be
Transitional Measures Act

confusion, if not chaos. My colleagues who are more intimately connected with the various phases of the matter could go into the thing more fully than I am prepared to do at the moment, but I think it is realized, whatever our views may be about controls, that this would be no way to end controls. To those who do not believe in controls at all on principle, the argument I think must be convincing that controls must be abandoned or dropped in a little more orderly way than this would be. To those who believe that there must be some measure of control in some of these fields for some time to come-and that is my belief-the importance of not permitting a lapsing of this control legislation on the twenty-ninth day of March is very great indeed. I am therefore moving the resolution.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Ilsley) has gone a long way in accepting the suggestions made during recent months by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken) and those on this side of the house, that statutes such as this which grant extraordinary and emergent powers should be brought to an end at the earliest possible day. I think consideration should be given to the repeal of the War Measures Act, another act in the same position as the National Emergency Transitional Powers Act; for as long as acts such as these stay on the statute book there is a continuing invitation to governments to utilize them and thereby abrogate the powers and prerogatives of parliament.
A lot of legislation has been introduced at this session and I think it has been passed with reasonable dispatch on the part of this parliament. When the minister spoke on February 4 last, as reported on page- 82 of Hansard, he set out in detail the various bills that were to be introduced by the government to take the place of orders in council. If it had not been for the fact that some other legislation was introduced which was not emergency .legislation, such as that dealing with the Chinese exclusion act, in my opinion there would have been no necessity for the minister to ask for any extension of this par-: ticular statute.
I think the time has come to put a stop to unnecessary departures from constitutional legislative practice and process. I think this is a step toward the restoration of the sovereignty of parliament over a bureaucracy noted by its multiplicity and even by its anonymities, a bureaucracy which in many cases is still above the law of this country, denied, as the individual is, the right of recourse to the courts against those acts that

are done to him individually and which he believes to be unjust. The minister might well continue the step he has taken today and make provision immediately to do away with those portions of the orders in council which deny the individual the right of recourse to the courts when at any time he is treated any differently by order in council or by regulation from others in the same class.
Our experience has shown that when you do not trust the courts, injustice and unfairness is the natural consequence. Now that we are taking this step forward, and a step forward it is, to deny extraordinary powers by way or order in council, I suggest to the Minister of Justice, through you, sir, that now is the time to show that, the emergency having passed, the courts of this country should be trusted to protect the rights of the individual. I am going to ask the minister when he gets the opportunity to take the house into his confidence in regard to whether or not parliament in fact has the power to pass this legislation at all.	.
At the time the bill was originally passed in the fall of 1945 the doctrine of emergency that had been enunciated in the privy council by Lord Haldane in 1922 and 1923 was still believed to authorize the dominion- parliament to entrench upon the legislative jurisdiction of the provinces under the guise or excuse of emergency. Within the last year a decision has been rendered by the privy council in the case of Attorney General for Ontario and the Canadian Temperance Federation. ' This case arose in connection with the Canada Temperance Act. I should like very much to have the minister explain how it can be justified under the excuse of emergency to pass large portions of the legislation that is being submitted to parliament, indeed the address that is now before parliament. If I understand that authority aright, and it has been interpreted on a number of occasions, not by the courts but by outstanding jurists and writers of jurisprudence, the doctrine of emergency no longer exists, and the excuse for the dominion parliament to entrench upon the legislative ambit of the provincial legislatures under the British North America Act no longer holds.
I intended to ask the minister to do what he has already indicated would be done, namely, to repeal or revoke all orders in council passed under the War Measures Act and continued under the National Emergency Transitional Powers Act as of March 31. That has been done. The other day I had occasion to suggest to the minister that he give us a list of all orders in council that were in effect

at the present time. I did that on March 14, and my remarks and the answer of the minister appear at page .1370 of Hansard. At the time it was impossible for the minister-or difficult, he said-to set forth in detail the orders in council that were in effect. Apparently now there is no necessity of having a list of those that are in effect and those that are being repealed, because all will be repealed as of March 31. But I am sure, sir, that I should not be denied the opportunity of saying this, that it was a serious situation that was revealed, that the people of Canada were subject to laws of which the cabinet was unable without great difficulty to set forth a list. We had an experience not so long ago of a secret order in council, and I am going to ask the minister when he replies to advise whether or not there are any other outstanding orders in council which will remain secret or are at present secret.

Next, if we pass this transitional bill covering a period of six weeks there is nothing to prevent the government from passing orders in council during that six weeks over and above those comprised as an appendix to the omnibus bill. Section 2 of the National Emergency Transitional Powers Act will still remain in effect, whereby the governor in council may make regulations and orders in council to facilitate the readjustment of industry and commerce, maintain and control and regulate supplies and services, prices, transportation, property, rentals, employment, salaries and wages, and so forth, and assist the relief of suffering and the restoration and distribution of essential supplies and services in any part of His Majesty's dominions or in foreign countries. I therefore think that the minister's declaration should go further and that he should undertake that no orders in council will be passed on and after March 31 under the powers contained in the act in regard to any matter other than those covered by the list of subjects and the orders in council appended to the omnibus bill, except by way of repeal of existent orders. I think too that he should give us the undertaking that in asking for this extraordinary undertaking departmental heads and officials shall be denied the right of passing regulations further and other than those now in effect.

In other words I want the assurance that the act will no longer be in effect except in so far as it is necessary to carry out the provisions made by the orders in council printed as an appendix to the omnibus bill. With that assurance, sir, we of the opposition are prepared to give support to the address that has been moved. It will mean that in giving that support parliament would now be making its declaration of supremacy and a declaration on the part of all of us that hereafter except in a very few matters the rule of bureaucracy in this country which continued throughout the period of the war and since will have come to an end.

Mr. Speaker, we are prepared to give support to this resolution. We believe that pending the passage of the omnibus bill it is essential that the government have power to continue controls in the interests of the Canadian people. We all remember the chaos that occurred in the United States about the first of July last year when their controls went out of existence because of the negligence of congress of that great country. The government of the United States at that time was unable to restore in very large measure the conditions that had existed prior to that period of chaos, and we would not be a party to anything that would bring about a similar condition in this country. Those of us who were in the United States last autumn when the president announced the removal of the remaining controls will remember the manner in which prices skyrocketed almost within a few hours of the removal of those controls.
As I listened to the discussion this afternoon and to the points made by the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) my mind went back to the period following the first great war. I remember how at the close of that war hon. gentlemen who now comprise the government of this country criticized very
Transitional Measures Act

bitterly the former administration because it had been necessary to utilize orders in council to do many of the things that must be done following a war of the magnitude of the war of 1914-18, as it had been following the second world war. I have in my desk at the moment one or two acts passed by my hon. friends to my right when they were in power from 1930 to 1935, such as the "blank cheque" legislation, the Natural Products Marketing Act and other acts of that kind giving the government of the day powers to pass orders in council to do many things which in the opinion of many of us should be done only by parliament. But it seems necessary that parliament must at times give authority to the government to do the things which it must do in an emergency.
I approach this question from a different point of view from that taken by the hon. member for Lake Centre. Parliament is sitting now, and I do not think the controls that have been lifted already during the sittings of this session should have been lifted without some discussion in this house. The cost of living has jumped during the last few months, and in my opinion this house should first have had the opportunity of discussing what should be done with regard to the controls which have already been removed.
As to the right of parliament to decide what shall be done, the bill which is to be introduced by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Ilsley) to secure from parliament powers in the fields covered by the omnibus bill is I think now the proper procedure for this house to follow. As far as this group is concerned we are not anxious to see the government destroy those controls which work to the benefit of the Canadian people. Indeed we should like to see some of the controls which have been removed put into effect again to improve the conditions of our people at this time. And so, Mr. Speaker, we are prepared to give the government this exten-tion of six weeks.
It has been suggested that this should not have been necessary had we not been dealing with other legislation which was inconsequential, but the only bill mentioned by the hon. member for Lake Centre as being in the latter category was the Chinese Immigration Act. As I recall it the discussion of that measure took only one day.

But so far as the old age pension order in council is concerned, no one suggests that it is on the way out. We hope it is on the way up. If the government's reply is that they can do better later when they get an agreement with the provinces, well and good. But let us not wait until that maximum of $50 a month, shall we say, is attainable. Mr. Speaker, the house is being asked for authority for the extension of the National Emergency Transitional Powers Act of 1945 as amended in 1946. I contend that the enforcement of the orders in council, should be a responsibility of the government of Canada instead of being left to the municipalities. By the time parliament deals effectively with this whole control matter the war will have been over for more than two years, and in the meantime all business is being hamstrung. Business men do not know what orders in council have been passed that are still not repealed. I know this because I have received letters from magistrates and other persons from which I gather that people have been fined under certain orders in council, and when I have looked them up, having gone to a great deal of trouble to search the records, I find that some of those particular orders under which people were convicted had
Transitional Measures Act

expired or had been repealed. The list of those still in effect should be published.
No business man can conduct his business satisfactorily today. The small business man is complaining of the handicap he i3 under through some of these irksome controls. It is all very well for certain hon. members to applaud and to support this legislation, but I can assure them that in the city of Toronto a large section of the police force is engaged in the enforcement of over 100,000 of these orders in council that should have expired right after the war was over. Take the housing situation. The summer will be gone before anything effective can be done by this parliament to aid it and remove some controls. The government has dilly-dallied with this question right along and it will not be before May 15, or four months after the first meeting of parliament, that we shall be able to deal with it. We might as well grant an extension to the end of the year of the whole act of 1945 as amended in 1946.
In the United States they got rid of their controls as quickly as they could. It is true that prices rose considerably for a short time, but they fell by the law of supply and demand when it was found that people were not buying the goods at the prices that were being charged. I do not see why these controls should be extended and played with by bureaucrats as they are in this country. As a member of parliament, I do not know what orders in council are still unrepealed, nor does the public know. I am sure the people do not want this legislation and a wide spread control system continued indefinitely. It leaves the administration and enforcement of these controls to the municipalities and is putting a burden on .the taxpayers. Building inspectors, architects and others engaged in that line cannot get on with their work because they do not know what the law is under all these various controls that have been set up. I would not object to a reasonable extension if an effort was made to eliminate them, but I hope that between now and May 15 all the unrepealed orders in council will be tabled.

The house resumed from Monday, March 17, consideration of the motion of Mr. Gardiner for the second reading of Bill No. 25, to provide for the sale and export of agricultural products.
Mr. JEAN -FRAN QOIS POULIOT (Temis-couata):	Mr. Speaker, this is a bill which
I have read with great care. We have been told so often that the ideal of the Liberal party was to give the private individual a chance that I am greatly surprised at this kind of legislation being sponsored, not by Mr. John Stracliey in England but by a Liberal government. I cannot conceive how a Liberal government would sponsor such legislation.
If what has been said about assistance to other countries of Europe is true, I would draw the attention of the minister to the first line of the preamble, where he will see that, whether inadvertently or not, the United Kingdom is not mentioned among the countries which were and still remain in grave distress for want of adequate food supplies. The question is not that of assistance to any other country, the United Kingdom, France or any other country. The question is whether this is a true democracy, whether we have private initiative any longer in this country, or have we a planned economy for good? We are told:	Oh, this is only for
a year-we will change it next year. How many times were we told during the war: This measure is only for the time of the war, and as soon as the war is over we will go back to normal. How many times did I tell the then leader of the opposition that he was wrong in that, that it was the duty of members of parliament to act as a brake to prevent this country from falling into ruins; and he said:	Well, I am patriotic and I
close my eyes during the war, but after the war we will see to it. The war has been over now for two years and still this thing is going on.

Agricultural Products Act
After all tlie denunciation we have heard of controls from all comers of the house I was surprised to see only thirteen members rise a moment ago to express their dissatisfaction with the continuance of controls. They speak one way and vote the other way. The members who are logical and have the courage to stand by their guns are very few in this house, and that is why parliament is falling into discredit in this country. It is because the actions of members of parliament are different from their public speeches. I want the Minister of Agriculture to understand very well that I am not discussing his case particularly. I am not discussing the case of the Right Hon. James Gardiner, Minister of Agriculture in the King government. I intend to discuss the case of any minister of agriculture. He will have control of all agricultural produce in this country except wheat, which is something formidable. He will have control even of the feed of animals. Did you ever think of that? I wonder how many members of parliament have read this legislation contained in Bill No. 25, establishing a special case, something that no one would have dreamed of in this country. Under it the Minister of Agriculture is being authorized by parliament to pass certain regulations and is being given by parliament more powers than any minister of agriculture ever had in any country.
Naturally the Minister of Agriculture will choose his own advisers. He will have power to buy and sell the agricultural produce of this country. He will have the right to establish boards, and he will have the right to tell every farmer in this country: "You will produce such and such agricultural product. You will sell it to me. If you do not sell it to me, you may be found guilty of an offence and sentenced to a fine or to jail, or to both." With the approval of the attorney general of Canada, who is the Minister of Justice (Mr. Ilslcv), and the attorneys general of the provinces, the fine may go up to $5,000 and the imprisonment to two years. The man who will not obey the order of the Minister of Agriculture may be sentenced to two years in jail and to pay a fine amounting to $5,000 as the maximum; because that man will not have obeyed the Minister of Agriculture, he will be found guilty. As a Liberal I cannot approve that.
We are supposed to pass legislation. I want legislation passed by this parliament-meaning passed through all stages in the House of Commons, the Senate and having the sanction of the Governor General-establishing what an offence is. That is the way it is done in tlie criminal code. Who ever gave a blank
cheque to anyone regarding the imposition of fines and imprisonment in this country? Where is the civil liberties league? We do not hear of them when we need them. We must do the work of the so-called civil liberties league. They are in existence only to defend rascals who have been traitors to this country.
Coming back to the bill, may I say that no farmer will approve it when it is explained properly to him. No farmer will say this bill is all right if he has an opportunity to read it. I know the farmers. I live among: them. They abide by the law but they want sensible laws. They want laws which appeal to their sense of justice. They do not want to receive orders from anyone. They will not understand why such immense powers have given to one man, however worthy he is of the confidence of his fellow citizens. Even if the Minister of Agriculture deserved the confidence of the whole house-and it is possible that he has it-he may die tomorrow, and his successor as minister of agriculture will have the very same powers, powers undreamed of by any Canadian public man. This is going to be done as a matter of course.
Yesterday excellent speeches were made by some of our colleagues who explained their points of view. Those who were in favour of the bill spoke very well too, but they did not convince me. It is said in the bill:
... it is necessary by reason of the existing national emergency that parliament-
That is all of us.
-confer authority to enable the government of Canada to fulfil its obligations.
In the dark, outside of parliament, the government of Canada has assumed tremendous obligations to other countries; and now we are called upon to give our sanction or approval to ail that. How is it that none of those agreements are published as an appendix to this bill? Some explanation may be given occasionally about it. We do not know what it is all about, and when we ask for some information we get it drop by drop. We have to fight for the information. It cannot be given properly because everything has been done in the dark. We have complained bitterly time and time again that parliament has been informed only after the thing has been done. We were informed of the accomplished fact. Parliament has never been consulted about the emergency-and I use the word which is used here-of passing such agreements with all other nations. And we are crazy enough to call it trade. It is the Santa Claus trade, with respect to food which is not paid for. When the words "sell and buy'' are used in this bill, it is only an optical
Agricultural Products Act

illusion. The minister will sell and buy nothing, in the legal sense of the word, but he will give away our birthright to other nations, because what will be given away by him will never be paid for by the other nations. It will be paid by the taxpayers of Canada; it will be paid by the farmers as well as by the labour men; it will be paid by the man in the street as well as by the millionaire. And now the minister is asking to be empowered with the authority to give away our birthright to all other countries, while there are people in this country who are badly in need of what he will give away.
I am strongly opposed to this. More than that, I take it quite seriously, and if I rise today I do so as a matter of duty. I do not rise for the pleasure of making a speech. When I make a speech it bores me as much as it does those who may listen to me. But I have a duty to fulfil, and I want to act in accordance with the solemn promise I gave my electors twenty odd years ago when I was elected. I told them that I would come here as a bulldog, one of the watchdogs of the treasury. That was a nickname that was given to me then and I never thought that one day I would be proud of it, as I am today.
Take the second section of the bill. All agricultural products except wheat-and even feeds are included in agricultural products- will be covered. The Minister of Agriculture is the one man who will deal with the agricultural reserve and agricultural production of the Canadian farmer. That must be well understood. What will he do? Subject to the reservation I have just made about the illusion of purchase and sale, there will be orders in council in virtue of which the minister may, first, sell or export agricultural products to the government of any country or any agency thereof, and, second, pursuant to agreements made by the government of Canada with the government of any such country or agency thereof, purchase or negotiate contracts for the purchase of agricultural products. This is a note I have made to make easier the understanding of the bill.
Not only is the minister empowered to buy according to the orders in council passed by this government, and also to sell accordingly, but there is a subsection which would not stand in any court. It is that we will empower the minister to purchase on behalf of the government of any country or any agency thereof-most incredible! Think of that, sir! Not only will the minister act on behalf of this country, but we empower him to act on behalf of other countries. What other countries? And what would he do? Third, by
fMr. Pouliot.]
order, he may require any person to give such information respecting his facilities for the storing or processing of agricultural products, and at such times, as the minister may designate in such order, and then enter into contracts for the storing or processing of agricultural products. That will be found in section 3 (c) and (d). This I find most despotic.

Well, sir, there are several principles involved in each section. However, I will demonstrate it to you. In the first place, I am opposed to this bill because it is a socialistic measure and I shall be unable to face my constituents and call myself a Liberal if I support this measure. They will tell me, "You are a member of the C.C.F.; you are a socialist; you are more socialist than the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar." That is why the hon. gentleman was so anxious to have a division yesterday, and to his great surprise some members voted against the bill on second reading-I mean the amendment. I beg your pardon, sir. Sometimes I make a slip, but too many thoughts come to my head.
Considering the principle, I am against socialism because I am for the right of the individual to try his luck in life, in the struggle for life. In my view it is the only reasonable chance that a man deserving to be called a man has to win success in life. That is the first point.
I am against a planned economy; I am against control. That is why I was one of the thirteen who voted against the so-called address presented by the Minister of Justice a moment ago. I am not only a Liberal; I am for the liberty of the individual. I am for the liberty of the individual to engage in trade and make a success of his business and contribute thereby to the prosperity of the state. That is my understanding of the whole problem.
That is principle No. 1, and the opposite is the planned economy sponsored by my hon. friends the socialists. When I say "socialists" I do not mean all the members of the C.C.F. group, because some of them are Liberals at heart.

That is one thing. Not only will the minister be the omnipotent master of all agricultural produce, but we give him the right to establish one or more commodity boards. How many there will be we do not know. He may authorize and require them to exercise and perform all or any of the powers and duties he is given under the previous section, with reference to such agricultural products as he may designate. Well, sir, that is formidable. Here again we have a delegation of power. We give the minister certain powers to establish boards, and then we will confer power upon those boards which aire not now in existence. We assume the responsibility for all those unborn babies of the Minister of Agriculture. If they do something wrong and a member
complains about it he will be told, "Well, on March 18, 1947, you voted for it, and you cannot complain now."
These are not the only institutions the minister may establish. He will have more than that. He will also have advisory committees, which he will select himself. There he will have these geniuses that the socialists are so fond of finding in large numbers in the civil service. It will be Pelion on Ossa, mountain upon mountain. There will be a mountain of agricultural products which will serve as a pedestal for the Minister of Agriculture. He will be on top of that mountain; and the number of bureaucrats making up the boards will have to be so great as to make a mountain just as high as the one on which the minister sits, in order that they may be in a position to confer with him about what they think the farmer needs. Not only that, Mr. Speaker, but the minister will dispense with the merit system and the civil service commission, and choose his own men. That is in section 7. In addition to that, the hon. member with the Scottish brogue (Mr. Bryce), who spoke last night about the Conservative member of parliament in Great Britain who made the statement that the farmers of Canada were trying to fleece the United Kingdom, did a very good job because he also defended the honour of this country.
The question is not one of sending agricultural products to any other country for re-export, for the benefit of traders over there, whoever they may be, under the false pretence of saying that it is done to alleviate the misery of the people. No. The point is that we must first look after our own people, and begin again to have real trade, trade under which exports are paid for, not by the taxpayers, but by the purchasers. If we cannot have trade of that kind, let us have barter.
I tell you, sir-and these are my concluding words-that the time is coming when we shall have two parties in this country. One will be an all-Canadian party, composed of people born either in this country or outside it- and that is of no importance. It will be composed of people who consider Canada as their paramount country, who consider Canada before any country of the world. On the other hand, we shall have a party composed of colonials, imperialists, Witnesses of Jehovah and members of the Ku Klux Klan-all the bums, and all the people who think differently and who are not bums, put together. The fight will be between Canadians and non-Canadians. And, judging by the feeling of the people, I am sure the Canadians will win. Mr. Speaker, I have listened with keen interest to the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot). I realize he needs no lessons with respect to the rules of procedure, because he has sat in the house for a long time, and comes of a family with wide parliamentary experience. It is many years since I first

Agricultural Products Act
listened to the hon. member in the House of Commons. But I can say to him now, sir, that this is the first time I have found myself in agreement with much of what he has said.
The main principles to which the hon. member referred-and the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) seemed to think the hon. member was referring to certain sections in the bill-are fundamental, and are seriously affected by the proposed legislation. I cannot agree with everything the hon. member said; indeed, some of his observations were not exactly relevant. I did not meet the two gentlemen to whom he referred as having been the advisers of the Right Hon. Mr. Bennett, when he was Prime Minister. That, however, is beside the point.
I feel that hon. members in this party ought not to be misunderstood either by Your Honour or by the Minister of Agriculture in respect of their attitude toward this marketing legislation. I believe that there is a great shortage of food, and that at the present time hunger exists in certain parts of Great Britain. There can be no doubt as to her need. Nor has anyone any serious doubt so far as Canada's obligation, if we may so describe it, is concerned. Whether we belong to the British commonwealth of nations or not, when the country which has taken so much of our products for so many years is in short supply, it is only prudent or sound business practice for us to endeavour to supply her with all the food we can possibly produce. Great Britain has been our greatest outlet for at least half a century. I believe there is no one in the house and perhaps but few in the country who do not appreciate the sacrifices Great Britain made during the war to save civilization. No member of the allied nations sacrificed so much during the war, and no member has suffered so much following it. Therefore I believe we might consider our part as that of a continuing ally in this post-war period.
Matters connected with trade have long since been the responsibility of the Department of Trade and Commerce. Yet we see that this bill is introduced by the Minister of Agriculture. I should have expected the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon) would have been its real father. The fact is, however, that it is presented1- one might say mothered-by the Minister of Agriculture.
We observe that it is to be effective for only a year. I do not know who will take the child at the end of that time. However, if hon. members to my left would care to adopt it I feel they would not want to change its manners very much. It will have been trained 83166-95
along the lines they approve, where every line of industry in the country would be strait-jacketed.
I do not believe the principle involved in this bill, whereby control is left in the hands of the minister, and through which he continues to make agreements, fix prices and tell us how much we are to receive for our products, is the best means of meeting the obligations which fall upon us as a member of the British commonwealth of nations.
I believe I can speak with some knowledge respecting the attitude of farmers; and in this I find myself in full agreement with the hon. member for Temiscouata who, I believe, understands the farmers in his district. One of the fundamentals which I have felt would be surrendered last by the farmer is his freedom of choice, and his right to do business in his own way, whether that way is or is not considered to be the most scientific by those who now seek to control his activities. I am satisfied that government policy during the last three or four years, and that government policy of today has been based upon a terrible fear of inflation. Price ceilings, controls and restrictions may have done something to avoid inflation, but what was done was done at the farmers' expense and it certainly did not help to provide food for Britain. Had we had higher prices for many lines of farm products, prices that were not arbitrarily fixed by controls, I am satisfied there would not be as manj' hungry people today in Great Britain.
Much has been said about what happened after the last war, but simply because something is said' loudly and emphatically in this house does not necessarily make it a fact. History shows that during the last war there was a greater percentage of increase in agricultural production than we had during this war. There was a great increase from 1915 to 1920 in preparation for the day when food would be short in Europe following the war. True the minister or any hon. member may say that we are producing more now than we did then. We produce more industrial products also. We are a quarter of a century older.
I recall, and I believe the Minister of Agriculture will recall that in 1921 we sent 255,000,000 pounds of bacon to England. We did not have a strait-jacket bill like this one. It is true that our farmers received high prices for that bacon; it is true the price was higher to the consumer, and I do not mean that we should take the last drop of blood from the British after what they have suffered. I am 100 per cent in favour of the donations that this country has made to Britain in the time

Agricultural Products Act

of her peril, but I submit that, had we had less fear of inflation, had there been higher prices for agricultural products, we would possibly have been in position to give Britain another $2,000 million which would represent little more than the loss we have taken in selling agricultural products under would prices.
There is no economist who has shown this house or this country that we are on the right road tow'ard finding a solution for the relief of the starving people of Europe, and Britain. No one can tell me that the production of eggs, butter and other lines of mixed farming products would have fallen during the last year had prices risen. If that is not the fact, then why was the ceiling removed from the price of eggs this week? I think our first duty is to find more food for what I would term our old customer, and anticipate as our future customer. It is the humanitarian duty of a great agricultural country like this to produce every pound of food we can.
True, the consumption of cereals is not as great as the consumption of many other lines. From 1913 and 1914 up to the present the British consumption of animal products, vegetables, fruits and many other lines of mixed farming products has been 150 to over 200 per cent above the consumption in 1912 and 1914, just before the first, great war. The present consumption of cereals is only 89 per cent of what it was during those years. It is natural that the products dealt with by this bill are those in which we can anticipate a growing market when more normal times return.	.
I consider that the minister is asking a great deal when he asks this house to pass a bill giving him the all-absorbing powTers referred to by the hon. member for Temiscouata. In order to avoid repetition I shall not go into the details because they have been discussed at length. As a farmer I reluctantly can conceive a situation arising where I shall have to ask the Minister of Agriculture when I can start seeding, how much I can sow and what I am going to get for the products I sell. There is a principle involved that is a vital one, and there is also a practical side to it.
What I am about to say I say in all sincerity because I do not want to arouse any bitterness at this stage of the debate. I am not speaking recklessly; I am speaking, as the hon. member for Temiscouata mentioned, more or less from a sense of duty to an agricultural riding, a duty to the people of this country. It is our duty as Canadians to do what we can to solve these terrible shortages. I should like someone to show me how you can have ceiling prices, sometimes at unattractive levels, and expect

to increase production. The old law of supply and demand has worked down through the years and increased prices have brought about increased production.
Reference has been made to the havoc and recklessness following the last great war. Some have referred to the United States of America having lifted their price ceilings, but I do not know that that affected the United States very greatly. United States farmers for two years now have received fifty per cent more for their agricultural products. I can see where they will be able to buy more tile drain, fences, steel roofs, and erect more buildings and thus keep the wheels of industry going by increased purchasing power.
I know that great emphasis has been placed upon what happened to the economy of this country after the last war, but that was not all caused by high prices. True, this kind of bill is a war baby; this kind of bill is what sometimes follows war. True, following the last war wheat rose to something like $3.25 a bushel, and it even sold for $3.40 a bushel at some points. The government of the day fixed the price of wheat and established the wheat board, but that board was discontinued when the war was over.
However, it gave the people an appetite for controls, planned economy if you will, for boards, regulations and a new economic doctrine. The same thing happened all over the world. In this country we had our wheat pools in western Canada, but I shall not go into that because they have been dealt with before. Then we had the fiasco of 1929 when we told the world what they would have to pay for our wheat. We all know the sad tragic story of what happened. That was about to be repeated in 1939. No one knows better than the Minister of Justice (Mr. Ilsley), that we were about in the same position as we were in 1929. Had it not been for the war, we would have had the same tragic results with reference to wheat.
If we are to strait-jacket every line of agriculture in Canada we are apparently starting with the industry which it was thought would be the last to be controlled. We thought the farmer was the one who was free. I have heard businessmen say that they were going to buy a farm because, if the government kept on getting more socialistic, or if another government even more socialistic came into power the farmer would be the last free man. Now we know he will be the first to be strait-jacketed; he will be the first to be put more or less under restraint. True,

Agricultural Products Act
we are told this is only for one year, but perhaps practice makes perfect and nothing corrupts like power unless it be more power.
I do not need to say that this bill involves a dangerous principle. It is not sound economically to place in the hands of any one minister power to fix prices and control the production and sale of agricultural products as this bill does. I do not think it was sound economically to carry price ceilings to the extremes we did and then expect our farmers to produce more when they had to sell their products at fifty per cent less than the United States farmers were getting just across the line. Our production in Canada would have been substantially higher but for those price ceilings. I know the Minister of Agriculture might reply:	Compare our production today
with what it was from 1930 to 1935 or from 1920 to 1925, and so forth. But he knows the answer to that. We all know how mechanization has revolutionized agriculture in recent years and resulted in greatly increased production in many lines. I wish that the hon. member for Middlesex West (Mr. McCubbin) was in the house at this moment. He and other farmer members would remember what happened in 1919 and 1920 and 1921. He would remember what prompted the farmers in those days to take loads of light hogs off the market and take them back home, as I did, and put seventy-five pounds more apiece on them. In those days the people of Europe were starving; the people of Britain were almost starving, and greater production was needed in Canada. There was the incentive of price and we produced more food and fats and lard for Britain and Europe. That is how we increased our production so enormously in those years; in 1921 we produced and sold 225,000,000 pounds of bacon. During four years in that period our production increased faster than in any three or four years in the last decade.
Even though the minister is asking for this power for only one year, it is not the type of power that should be placed in the hands of any one minister. It is another illustration of the dangerous trend we see in these days, similar to the socialistic trends that started to develop not only in Canada but overseas following the first great war. We know the history of Russia in the years from 1917 to 1920 and how the same phrases were used then. They talked of getting parity between town and village, and then everybody would be happier and production would be increased. But it was Lenin himself who said that that policy had failed and Russia returned to the policy of giving her people returns according 83166-95J
to what they produced. We all know how in Germany democratic socialism grew into nazism. We all know what started fascism in Italy. But whether it be fascism in Italy or democratic socialism in Germany, then later nazism, or whether it be so-called socialism in Canada, it all leads eventually to the one thing, and that is a totalitarian state governed by a bureaucracy. Surely after twenty years of experience the time has arrived when we should stop, look and listen before we sow even the kernel of that kind of seed in Canada. I have been amazed to hear people say that we should have a planned economy in Canada; that we should not have any big businesses, and the government should take them over. This kind of socialist legislation that we have before us is the seed that brings forth that type of fruit.
My hon. friends to my left have suggested that we have not enough controls. They believe that some businesses are too big, and yet they assume that they are big enough themselves to run them all.
It has often been glibly said in this house that we have just come through a war that was caused by the capitalists, but proclaiming it loudly does not constitute it a fact. The wrar was a socialist engendered war. The socialists brought in the sword and perished by the sword.
So far as I am concerned I propose to vote against this measure. Reluctantly I acquiesced in extending the emergency powers of the government for another month. I believe that even that is more than they should have asked for. But when it comes to this measure, Mr. Speaker, I say in all sincerity that I can never be a party to putting into any minister's hands or the hands of any department or of any government the, control of the individual such as is sought in this legislation, whereby the government would be in a position to tell the farmer: You will obey me; you will do as I say; you will sow7 what I command and you will reap what I tell you; you will sell at my price; and if you do not follow my orders you will be committing an offence for which you may be fined up to $5,000 and be sentenced to gaol for two to five years. That is going a very long way in controlling other people's lives. We are taking some wild economic chances, but this is one power that I am not going to give to the minister, and if I do nothing else I know that, in taking that stand, I am representing the people who have elected me. We must return to sane and sound common sense. Call it free enterprise, individual initative; call it liberty, freedom, or anything you like-that is the system under which this country has developed and pros-

Agricultural Products Act
pered and that is the system we should follow, not socialism, not C.C.F.ism or any other ism, because all these isms eventually mean the same thing or nothing at all. We must return to the truth enunciated in the Scriptures and earn our bread by the sweat of our brow and receive reasonable recompense for services rendered.
I think the minister will be well advised to review the agreements he has made with Britain. I hope he makes no more of the kind he has made. As a member from Montreal said the other day: Now that we are buying and selling as a nation, we are dealing in national cartels and if any fault is to be found against us for what is done under these agreements it will not be the Winnipeg grain exchange that will be charged or the live stock dealers; it will be Canada herself, because it is this nation that will be dealing with Britain.
I say, Mr. Speaker, that we can produce more food and send more food to Britain if the farmer is allowed to run his own business. The harder he works, the more he expects to earn; and higher prices should bring greater production. That greater production should adjust prices so that the British consumer will not be hurt. Canada's economy cannot afford such novel agreements whereby we are forced to sell our products at less than world prices. This country must maintain a sounder type of economy to be able to play her part in the British commonwealth of nations.

not brought up in a home where "shut up" was permitted to be said. However I am not dealing with that now.
Members of parliament have a tremendous responsibility in this complex and befuddled world. We might talk about nails and they are important to the builder who cannot get any. We might talk about fish traps. We might even talk about the increase in the price of agricultural products, and certainly the farmers have a right to expect all they can get for their production. Those things are important to the people who might be involved. But even those things are important matters of but passing interest. What I am trying to put over here is that the responsibility of members of parliament, as they scrutinize legislation, is to ask what effect it will have upon the nation or upon the world, because we are one unit in the world of nations. Consideration must be given to the effect this or that legislation will have upon the world twenty, fifty, one hundred or even a thousand years from now. The great statesmen of the past have always done things in the light of the effect on future generations. Any legislation which is to fit into a programme purposely designed to bring about a world socialist authoritarian state must be looked upon with tremendous care and given the closest scrutiny.
I notice that some hon. members have been urging the minister to make promises as to what he is going to do a year from now with respect to agriculture. I am not one of those. I believe we should have some adequate marketing legislation, but it should be marketing legislation which will put the power where it belongs, namely in the hands of those who produce and have the production for sale, not in the hands of powerful bureaucrats. I am not asking the minister to make any promises about future legislation. We will deal with that when we come to it. As far as my small voice is concerned, if I see anything in legislation which fits into this evil scheme of things I shall raise my voice in opposition. Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to take up the time of the house very long, but as a farmer and a representative from an agricultural constituency I feel I must add my voice in protest against this bill.
The farmers in my part of the country are already restless under the controls which now exist, and they are fearful of seeing any more controls come into effect. They have seen controls lifted, and have seen other classes released from controls; and they fear that with this bill the chains which already bind them are going to be strengthened. They feel, and I agree with them, that we cannot live half
[Mr. CoIdweJI.J
bond and half free. That is why I am so much afraid that measures of this kind will in time lead to complete socialism and dictatorship. You cannot control one thing without its affecting a great many others. The farmers I know are demanding that the government stop their ears and steer away from this siren song of socialism.
As the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe) pointed out this afternoon, too many ships of state have already been lured to their doom by those seductive strains. I fear that this bill will defeat the very purpose for which it is intended, namely to produce more foodstuffs for Great Britain. One needs only to look around Ontario today, to see the acres and acres of fat farm land that is growing nothing but weeds, to look at the acres and acres of good farm land being only half worked, to look at the thousands of young men who are leaving the farms and going to jobs where they can earn twice as much money for half the work, to realize the truth of what I am saying.
Look at the reduced production in many lines; and if more restrictions are put on the farmers it will result only in more restricted production. I feel-and I speak only for myself, although I am sure there are others on both sides of the house, in addition to the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot), who feel the same-that this thing we are letting ourselves in for, this incipient socialism, is nothing but the beginning of a cancer. If at the beginning it is not destroyed, root and branch, it will continue to grow until it destroys us. To remove it will require a major operation, an operation which will be painful and which many people dread. But unless we do operate and root it out, it will destroy the way of life we now have.

GARDINER (Minister of Agriculture): Mr. Speaker, when last Monday evening the second reading of this bill was called I had thought I might save time by not speaking on second reading. Agricultural Products Act
however, I was mistaken in that; and probably mistaken in something else, that I had placed in the hands of the opposition the evening second reading was called an amendment which was suggested from the other side of the house, rather than from this side. That has caused a considerable amount of debate to take place on the second reading that probably might better have come in committee.
In view of the discussions which have taken place, I think it is necessary that I should say something before the vote is taken. I am not going to follow the criticism which was made this afternoon from this side of the house by the hon. member for T emiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) other than to say that no one has suggested that anything which was done during the war period under the powers given by the orders in council that are dealt with in this legislation -was part of Liberal policy or principle.
I have stated on previous occasions that the Liberal party -was established in Britain for the same purpose that some other organizations are being established in these days; it was established during the last century for the purpose of trying to make wars unnecessary and impossible. It was not established for the purpose of conducting or prosecuting wars; it was established for the purpose of avoiding them. In other words, it had in mind that a situation would be created of extending among the peoples of the world the opportunity of trading freely with one another which would make war not only unnecessary but impossible. It may be that time has disappointed some of those who were strong advocates of that idea; nevertheless I think something has happened as a result which has been really beneficial.
When war did come in 1939 no one thought that war could be conducted under a condition where there would be freedom of exchange of goods as among the countries of the world. The first thing that had to be stopped was freedom of the exchange of goods among the countries of the world. It was stopped,, not only by the armies but by every kind of regulation that could be put on to stop it. So we had to stop trading with countries with which we had previously been trading, and with which we have not yet got back to trading. I repeat that Liberalism was never established for the purpose of prosecuting wars and it cannot be utilized for the purpose of successfully carrying on a war when once we are forced into it.

If that remark was
intended to reflect on the government, I am quite sure we made a better job of it than did the Conservative party in the previous war. During the war certain agreements were made, and may I say that those agreements were not made with a socialist government. The agreements which are before this house under this legislation were made at a time when the present leader of the Conservative party in Great Britain was in charge of the government and when the minister of food in that country, Lord Woolton, was one of the outstanding leaders of the Conservative party. Negotiations for the agreements which are before the house under this legislation were mostly between Lord Woolton and myself and our officials in London. They were then carried on later by his representatives and ours both in Ottawa and in London. I say to hon. members opposite and to hon. members on this side, who criticize Mr. Strachey and other members of the British government that they are not criticizing the persons with whom these agreements were entered into. These agreements were entered into with the government that prosecuted the war under the leadership of Mr. Churchill.
Having said that, may I call attention to some of the criticism which we have had, not only during this debate but at other times, with regard to the activities of this government. We have been told that during the war period we appointed too many boards. We have been told that this country should operate under a responsible representative system of government and that the ministers should take responsibility. I have sat in my place in this house during all the years of war and listened to the official opposition hammering Donald Gordon, for example, and suggesting that the powers which were in his hands should be in the hands of the Minister of Agriculture. I have heard hon. members on both sides of the house contend that the powers which were put in the hands of the different boards ought to be in the hands of the ministers themselves. Now, when some effort is made on this occasion to retain some of the responsibility in the hands of the ministers we hear nothing but criticism of that particular action from ' the official opposition.
Then both prior to and during the debate we have heard many statements to the effect that we should do away with compulsion, more particularly compulsion that is exercised by bodies outside the government itself. Again I say that in this debate we have heard a constant advocacy of the idea of setting up an independent board of some
Agricultural Products Act

kind and giving to that board all the authorities which this bill places in the hands of the government itself.
Then it was said by the leader of the
opposition, as reported at page 260 of Hansard:
I am sure also that the house will be pleased to know from the minister's statement that no extension of powers is proposed but rather an extension of time during which certain controls will continue, approximately a year, I understand. We will examine the measure very carefully with respect to the statement that there is not an extension of powers. I hope we will find that that is correct.
Almost every time that hon. members of the official opposition have been on their feet they have been advocating the extension of powers that were given to the Minister of Agriculture or to the different boards or to the government itself under the orders in council that were passed during the period of the war. So I say that this debate has somewhat surprised and astonished me in the course that it has followed.
Probably I should now ask some questions with regard to the measure that has been discussed continuously ever since this debate opened as the measure that ought to be adopted by the house. I wish to thank the hon. leader of the C.C.F. party for having read mto the record certain clauses from the bill that was introduced into this house in 1934 by the official opposition. I should like to read into the record some of the proposals which have been made in this debate and which, it has been suggested, ought to be adopted. I am afraid that every member of the opposition voted for them last night.
We have had the suggestion made that certain things ought to be done in this house at the present time because farm organizations have asked for them. I have in my hand the model bill which the farm organizations have asked for. On the second page is a list of the names of the heads of most of the farm organizations in Canada, and then the short title of the bill is given as follows:
This act may be cited as the Farm Products Marketing Act.
Then under interpretation:
(c)	"Marketing" means with respect to interprovincial trade within Canada or export trade, preparing for sale, buying and selling and offering for sale, or otherwise disposing of any farm product in any manner whatsoever, and includes its transportation in any manner by any person.
You could hardly have an interpretation of marketing which could be wider than that. Then it goes on to give the purpose and intent of the act as follows:
The purpose and intent of this act is to provide in respect to interprovincial trade in Canada and in export trade, for the improvement

of the methods and practices of marketing of farm products, and for the promotion control, regulation, or prohibition, of the marketing of farm products, in any or all respects and in whole or in part.
The next section is headed, "Establishment of schemes and marketing boards", and reads:
The governor in council shall establish a board to be known as the dominion marketing board.
It does not say that the farmers are to establish a board but the governor in council is to establish a board. Then it goes on to say:
(a) The board shall consist of such number of persons as the governor in council may from time to time determine, and each member shall hold office during pleasure and shall receive such remuneration-
Not such remuneration as the farmers decide to give him, but :
-as the governor in council shall determine.
Then paragraph (i) says:
(1)	The governor in council may from time to time authorize payment to the board out of moneys to be appropriated by parliament of such sums of money as may be necessary to assist in the organization of local boards, to defray the operating expenses of the board incurred by it directly and any expenditure incurred or authorized by the board.
Then section 2 goes on to say:
(2)	On recommendation of the board, the governor in council may, from time to time establish, amend and revoke schemes for the marketing or the promoting, regulation or prohibition of the marketing of any farm product, in the interprovincial trade within Canada and in export trade, and may constitute local boards to administer such schemes.
All of this is based on orders in council, as is customary with all such legislation brought before the house.
Then we come to the powers of the board in section 5:
5. (1) Without limiting the generality of any of the other provisions in this act, the governor in council may, subject to the provisions of this act and in respect to interprovincial trade within Canada and of export trade, vest in the dominion marketing board, any or all of the following powers:-
(a) To market or to regulate the time and place at which, and to designate the agency by or through which, any regulated product may be marketed; to regulate, control, or determine the manner of distribution, the quantity, quality, variety, grade, class, or size of the regulated product which shall be marketed by any person at any time; and to prohibit the marketing of any quantity, quality, variety, grade, class or size of any regulated product.
You can tell them that they cannot market their small potatoes and small apples; that they cannot market this and cannot market that. I am not saying that this is legislation which ought to be passed or ought not to be

Agricultural Products Act
passed, but when members of the opposition talk about the powers given by order in council to boards or by order in council to ministers or by order in council to anyone, there is in this bill no power over the individual which compares with the powers proposed in the bill that was suggested to this house last night and was voted for by every member of the opposition who was then in the house. Then paragraph (h) gives the board power:
(h) To require full information relating to the marketing of the regulated product from all persons engaged therein, and to require periodic returns to lie made by such persons; and to inspect the books and premises and vehicles of such persons.
Then paragraph (k):
(k) To require the person in charge of any vehicle to stop the vehicle and to permit any person appointed by the board for such purpose, to inspect the vehicle and its contents.
All these powers and many more-the paragraphs exhaust the greater part of (he letters of the alphabet up to (o)-can be brought into being and would be brought into being, not by any farm organization, but by order in council and would be put into effect by the government of the day. All I wish to say in that regard, in reply to the suggestion that under the present legislation wide powers are given to the government and the minister, and through the minister to boards, is that there are contained in this bill no powers which begin to compare with those contained in the bill that was proposed to set up a permanent marketing board.
In addition, criticism was made of the penalties. In this bill the penalties do not exceed $5,000, whereas in the model bill the penalties run from $25 to not more than *10,000.
Having said that with regard to the legislation that has been proposed, may I now say something with regard to the powers contained in the present bill which have been severely criticized by those discussing the bill. I agree with the leader of the C.C.F. party when he says that, in spite of the fact that these agreements are to be carried out with a British government which for the time being is socialist, this legislation is not socialist in most of its clauses. There may be some respects in which it may be termed socialist to a degree, but I quite agree that it is not the kind or type of legislation which the C.C.F. party, if they were in, power in this country, would introduce into this house. It has in it some principles with which they agree and it deals with a situation now existing in a manner with which they agree, but it is not a bill which is
based on the principles of socialism any more than the bill which the official opposition advocated in 1934 and advocated again last night is based entirely or even largely on the principles of socialism.

The second thing which
is proposed in this act is to give the government the power to go out and make a new agreement with regard to apples and to have the authority to make new arrangements with regard to such matters as beef, if it is found necessary to do so, in order to take care of the situation in this country. But as far as I know at the present time we shall probably not change our mind with regard to sending quotas of beef into the United States, for the same reason I spoke of the other night. But there could be developments in our relationship with the Americans, from thoughts expressed to us by them, which might change our minds with regard to a matter of that kind.
Discussions have gone far enough to indicate why we have special provision made in the bill to take care of apples. I have not any hesitation in saying that if it is the will of this house-and I am speaking more particularly to the opposition-and if they want the provisions for dealing with apples and the provisions for dealing, if necessary, with cattle, or any other condition of that kind removed from this bill. I have not any objection to its being removed. It will take only one word to remove it, and that word can be put in when

Agricultural Products Act
we come to the section where it can be put in, and it will remove entirely from the act any necessity for dealing with anything new in connection with this bill.
I say I am prepared to do that, and I have not any hesitation in saying why I am prepared to do that. The government have given every consideration to the representations which have been made to them through the Minister of Agriculture by producers of cattle and by producers of apples; and we have placed in the bill, as I said the other night, a degree of increased authority and power in order to make it possible for us to go that much farther. But if. when we get into committee, this house wants that power taken away, I am not going to battle in order to retain that position, in the light of what has been said in the discussions throughout this debate. We can have everything which is necessary to be done under the agreements which we have made, because every other one of these orders in council preparing for the setting up of boards, except that having to do with meat, confines our activities entirely to the United Kingdom and does not make it possible for us to do any trading under these agreements with any country but Great Britain. The meat order do.es make it possible for us to deal with other countries.
One thing which is necessary before we can deal with apples as we did deal with them during the war, is to have some authority with regard to interprovincial trade. We do not require any authority with regard to interprovincial trade in order to deal with the other agreements which were already made under the orders in council which we had during war time.
I want to state clearly, Mr. Speaker, to the members of the house that the one thing which involves principle in connection with this bill is the provision for carrying out the contracts which we have made, giving us the authority to change price levels and quantities in those contracts until we reach the end of the period covered by the contracts. In addition to that, we have said that we are prepared to come back here once a year and report on what has happened. We are not saying that we are not going to ask the house for an extension of these powers next year. We have said clearly that we likely shall be doing that because our contracts on meat, bacon, beef and cheese, as well as on other products, will run beyond March 31. 1948; and unless something happens which makes it absolutely impossible for this country and Britain to continue their contractual relationship, we shall be back a year from now asking
for an extension of these authorities under the bill. But this house will have the power then to deal with them just as they have the power to deal with them now. However the principle underlying this bill, and the only principle which the government has been insistent upon putting into it and keeping in it, is the authority which is necessary to carry out the agreements we have made to deliver our surpluses of food to the United Kingdom. If we have this in the bill when it is completed, we shall consider that we have reached the objective we have in mind; and I would suggest that the bill be given its second reading.

We did make inquiries as to whether we could obtain potatoes for another purpose which I do not feel free to discuss at the moment. The report I have had is that we shall not obtain the quantity of potatoes required, and so I have concluded that there were not so many surplus potatoes in the maritimes as we thought there were a month ago.

Yes, I agree with them or I would not have brought this bill in. The reason given was that you could not possibly handle the situation which exists this year under the type of marketing bill which we would want in Canada, over a long period; and that if you had put on the statute books, in addition, any other marketing bill that we might approve at all, whether it conformed with the wishes of the opposition or not, it would only be putting a third piece of legislation on the statute books at the present time to deal with the situation. We have the Agricultural Prices Support Act which now makes it possible for us to keep a floor under any farm product, and it makes it possible for the government to do that by taking money out of the treasury. No farm organization could do that directly. The government must tax the people, take the money out of the treasury and utilize it for the purpose of doing certain things. We said, by act of this parliament in 1944-and that act is on the statute books-that we are prepared to utilize that act for the purpose of seeing to it that the farmer is not punished because he took the prices which he did take during the time we were controlling ceilings. I think that act

But he could not buy them. They did not exist. Those of us who wanted to buy farm implements, tractors and all the other equipment which a farm needs, could not buy those items throughout the war; and up until now we have not been able to buy them in the numbers which we want to. That being the case, we did not get the full advantage of the controlling of prices downward. When it comes to textiles, any farmer member knows that does not mean as much to farmers as it does to people engaged in other occupations in this country. Farmers wear overalls, work boots and rough clothing. They dress up once a week in other clothing and their suits last a long time. It is not the same saving for a man on a farm to have textiles held down for a period as it is to some other people; but even when the farmer wanted to buy textiles he could not, and so he has now come to the period when his clothing is worn out and his implements are worn down. My contention is, therefore, that the transitional legislation ought to see him through that situation; and our bill, which we put in to take care of that situation, ought to remain on the statute books and we should not substitute anything else for it, nor should we be transferring the responsibility of the Government to some farm organzation. The government should assume that responsibility until we have got through the transitional period.
That being so, I doubt very much whether I could draft a bill or have one drafted. I know I could not draft it, but I doubt very much whether I could state the principles to someone who would draft it in legal terms clearly enough to avoid doing harm to the legislation we already have on the statute books and which, I think, must stay there for a time.
Let me say, however, that we have not been idle in that regard. I instructed my officials, not this year, but two or three years ago, that we had representations from farm organizations, just prior to the war and again during the first year of the war, to the effect that this

legislation would be wanted, that all the provinces have it, and that we ought to be working on the possibility of having a bill, though not necessarily the bill that has been proposed. I do not know whether I would want to introduce a bill like that. If we could get one couched in some other terms, which would do the job more to my satisfaction and, I believe, to the satisfaction of the majority of the farmers than even the legislation which the farmers' organizations propose, then I would bring that in rather than any bill which they suggest. I do not want it understood that we have not been giving thought to the question. We have had men working on it, and after having them working on it we have come to the conclusion that, no matter what bill we might desire to bring in, we would not wish to bring it in this year, and that necessitates our giving it at least another year's consideration.

Mr.	GARDINER:	That	is the	1934	act?Mr.	CHARLTON:	That	is the	draft	act,Mr.	GARDINER:	Of	1934?Mr.	CHARLTON:	No;	that is	the draft

It has been said, as I pointed out before, that the Natural Products Marketing Act of 1934 gave just as much power to the governor in council as this Bill No. 25. It does not. It puts power in the hands of producer boards, or the local boards as they are called. One section was read last night by the hon. member for Dauphin, but if he had read further he would have found that the governor in council was given authority as set out in these terms:
On recommendation of the board, the governor in council may. from time to time, establish, amend and revoke, schemes for the marketing or the promoting, regulation or prohibition of the marketing of any natural product, in interprovincial trade within Canada and in export trade, and may constitute local boards to administer such schemes, and may vest in those local boards respectively any powers considered necessary or advisable to enable them effectively to market or to promote, control, regulate. or prohibit such marketing of any natural product, in any or ail respects and in whole or in part.
And listen to this:
Such schemes may only be established when evidence lias been submitted to the board that the schemes are favoured by a satisfactory proportion of producers in the area affected.

-the farmers to bind themselves under a central marketing agency to fill the contract.

Provision is made in section 4 (1) for the minister to establish one or more commodity boards. The word "may" is used before the word "establish" which makes it permissive rather than obligatory. Then, further down, so far as I can see there is no provision made for any producer representation on the boards so named. I believe the representations made here were fairly unanimous to the effect that the producers concerned should have some control of or at .least some say in the manner in which their products should be handled. Therefore I would move this amendment to section 4 (1):
That subsection 1 of section 4 of said bill be deleted and the following substituted therefor:
"(1) The governor in council shall establish one or more commodity boards with adequate producer representation and may authorize and require a commodity board to exercise and perform all or any of the powers and duties of the minister under section 3 of this act with reference to such agricultural products as the governor in council may designate; but in the exercise of such powers and duties a commodity board shall be subject to the direction and control of the minister."
The changes are two in number. First the word "may" is replaced by the word "shall", which makes it mandatory that the minister shall appoint the boards. The second change, and the one I consider most important, is that the words "with adequate producer representation" are included in the subsection. In this way it appears to me we shall be combining ministerial responsibility with producer representation on the boards. I believe the acceptance of this amendment would meet the wishes of all hon. members.
